chunks: He said: Abu Hafs Umar ibn Muhammad, known as Ibn al-Zayyat, narrated to us from Ali ibn Mahrwayh al-Qazwini, from Dawud ibn Sulayman al-Ghazi, from al-Ridha Ali ibn Musa, peace be upon them both, who said: My father Musa ibn Ja'far narrated to me, who said: My father Ja'far ibn Muhammad narrated to me, who said: My father Muhammad ibn Ali narrated to me, who said: My father Ali ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, who said: My father al-Husayn ibn Ali, peace be upon them all, said: The Commander of the Faithful, peace be upon him, said:
"If a servant of God could see his appointed time of death and how swiftly it advances towards him, he would detest all his vain hopes and abandon the pursuit of worldly life."

He said: And Abu al-Faraj al-Barqi al-Dawudi recited to me, saying: A saintly old man who had secluded himself in devotion to God the Exalted at Bayt al-Maqdis recited to me: "One who waits for death every hour, yet diligently constructs, builds, and fortifies; He has the conviction of a certain believer when reality tests him, yet his deeds are those of one who has no certainty; Manifest yet denied, his knowledge is like ignorance, in his ways regarding all that he claims to be certain of."
And may God bless our master Muhammad, the Prophet, and his pure progeny.

key_terms.الأجل: Ajal - the appointed time of death, a fixed term decreed by God
key_terms.الأمل: Amal - long hopes and worldly ambitions that distract from the hereafter
key_terms.الدنيا: Dunya - the worldly life, often contrasted with the akhirah (afterlife)

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Ali say about the appointed time of death and worldly ambitions?
ai.summary: Imam Ali (peace be upon him), through a golden chain of narration passing through all the Imams, warned that if a person truly saw how quickly death approaches, they would abandon worldly ambitions. The hadith, transmitted at the 36th gathering (majlis) of al-Shaykh al-Mufid, is followed by ascetic poetry from a devout elder at Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) that laments human contradiction: people claim certainty about death yet act as though it will never come.
